title: The Morley Triangle is Largest at the Equilateral

problemStatement.formal: For fixed circumradius R, the Morley side 8R·sin(α/3)sin(β/3)sin(γ/3) over triangles (α+β+γ=π, α,β,γ>0) is maximized at α=β=γ=π/3 with value 8R·sin³(π/9).
problemStatement.plain: Among all triangles with a fixed circumradius, which has the largest Morley equilateral triangle? Answer: the equilateral triangle; maximal side = 8R·sin³(π/9) ≈ 0.32008 R.
whyMatters: Sharp extremal characterization of the Morley side-length formula, orthogonal to OQ-01 (Conway construction) and OQ-02 (second Morley triangles)
Fully elementary: AM-GM(3) plus Jensen for sin, no calculus or Lagrange multipliers
Note: the originally-seeded OQ-03 (contribute cosine_rule_identity to Mathlib) was vacuous — that identity is already fully proven in MorleysTheorem.lean

knownResults.goal: Prove the Morley side length is maximized (for fixed R) exactly at the equilateral triangle.

insights: Substituting aᵢ=αᵢ/3, the constraint α+β+γ=π becomes a₁+a₂+a₃=π/3, so the trisected-angle mean is always π/9 regardless of the triangle.
Maximizing the Morley side reduces to maximizing ∏ sin(αᵢ/3) at fixed sum π/3, whose max is at the equal point by concavity+AM-GM.
Two-step bound: ∏ sin aᵢ ≤ ((Σ sin aᵢ)/3)³ ≤ sin(π/9)³ (AM-GM then Jensen), numerically verified with 0 violations.
Strict uniqueness extracted from the bound proof: equality sandwiches ((Σsin)/3)³ = sin(π/9)³, then pow_left_inj₀ (a^n=b^n↔a=b on nonnegatives) gives (Σsin)/3 = sin(π/9), i.e. Jensen is tight.
Tight Jensen ⟹ angles equal handled by sin_jensen_three_eq, which reads the equality case off each chained 2-point step via strict concavity (strictConcaveOn_sin_Icc.2).
R>0 is essential for uniqueness: at R=0 every triangle has Morley side 0, so the maximizer is not unique.
